newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin defends powers, objects to NATO plan.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin defends powers, objects to NATO plan.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin, in a bid to show firm control over Russia despite bad health, on Friday rejected calls by political foes to give up some of his powers and reiterated Moscow's opposition to NATO's expansion.

Kremlin spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky said Yeltsin, 66 on Saturday, discussed the issues at meetings with his chief of staff Anatoly Chubais and Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov in a residence outside Moscow where he is recovering from pneumonia.

Yastrzhembsky told a news briefing that Yeltsin, whose bad health had prompted concerns about his ability to rule Russia, opposed proposals to amend the 1993 constitution to pass some of his powers to parliament and the government.

"The president cannot agree with such proposals," Yastrzhembsky said. "In his opinion the constitution...has shown it can work, played and still plays an important stabilising role in society," he added.

"The president thinks that we must learn to live under the current constitution, to use its potential to the full extent and only after that it may become possible to decide with cool head whether any changes are needed at all."
Yastrzhembsky said that Yeltsin confirmed at the meeting with Primakov his opposition to the Western alliance's plan to grant full membership to some of Moscow's Cold War allies in Eastern Europe.
Moscow opposes NATO's enlargement, saying it would threaten its security and cause new divisions in Europe.

"Russia consistently sticks to its (negative) position," Yastrzhembsky said when asked whether a meeting between Primakov and NATO Secretary General Javier Solana earlier this month had softened Russia's opposition.
"It is clear that there is a consensus among Russia's political elite on key foreign policy issues," Yastrzhembsky said. "This includes oppsition to NATO's expansion."
Yastrzhembsky said the dispute would be high on the agenda when Yeltsin meets French President Jacques Chirac in Moscow on Sunday.
He suggested Moscow saw some hope in the fact that France is sometimes at odds over NATO's development with the United States, a staunch proponent of the expansion plans.
Yastrzhembsky told reporters that the two leaders would "compare approaches to the creation of a new security architecture in Europe. We have much in common on this respect."
"NATO will also be discussed. As you know, the position of France differs somewhat from that of Washington and Bonn."
Paris opposes any Russian veto on European security, but an official in Paris said: "We will plead Russia's case in NATO."

The official said Paris supported Moscow's demands for a binding charter on Russia-NATO relations and felt the United States was still trying to fob off the Russians with a few, non-binding pledges. Washington and most NATO allies oppose a legally binding accord requiring parliamentary ratification.
Chirac hopes NATO can work out a deal with Russia before NATO holds a summit in Madrid in July, at which it is expected to issue invitations to some eastern European countries.
Yeltsin's meeting with Chirac will be the second with a Western leader since his bypass surgery on November 5.

Yeltsin has made only three visits to the Kremlin since he left hospital on January 20. Brief footage of him on television has done little to ease doubts over his health sparked by two heart attacks in 1995.

Heart problems have kept Yeltsin away from his office for most of the period since he won a second four-year term last July. He had a multiple bypass operation in November and then went down with double pneumonia on January 8.

Kremlin officials say that Yeltsin, whether being treated in hospital or convalescing in country residences, has been kept informed about the state of affairs in Russia and continues to control the country.

His opponents argue that economic and social problems in the country, where tens of millions people have not been paid for months, and pressing international issues such as NATO's plans to expand eastwards, demand more efforts from the leader.
